subject: Post-demo: parallel connection SLAs & adaptive burst window proposal
messages:
From: Laura Bennett <laura.bennett@redwood.com>
To: Kyle Mercer <kyle.mercer@finledger.com>, Priya Shah <priya.shah@finledger.com>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>
Date: Wed, 12 Jun 2029 09:17:00 -0700
Subject: Post-demo: parallel connection SLAs & adaptive burst window proposal

Hi Kyle / Priya —

Thanks for joining the demo this morning. Quick recap from our side and an initial proposal to align on concurrency and burst behavior so you can validate architecture with your infra team. High-level notes below; I attached a suggested ratecard and your network topology screenshot that you shared.

Key goals we heard:
- End-to-end 95th pctl latency target of 350ms for single-request text generation (avg token length ~60).
- Sustained throughput target of ~450 QPS for the core payment validation endpoint during batch hours, with spiky bursts up to ~2,500 parallel requests for 90s windows during peak batch settlement.
- Streaming requirement for long-running workflows (server-sent chunking) where analysis results emit progressively — expect up to 300 concurrent streaming sessions.

Proposed Redwood baseline (for initial pilot):
1) Sustained parallel connections: reserve 500 ephemeral parallel streams (connection slots) mapped to your production endpoint.
2) Adaptive burst window: allow a burst pool of 2,000 extra concurrent request slots for a rolling 120s window with automatic smoothing back to baseline (this prevents hard failures during the 90s spikes you described).
3) Streaming sessions: allocate 300 streaming session slots; streaming sessions consume a streaming slot + 1 ephemeral parallel request for initial handshake.
4) Token throughput guardrails: soft throttles at 60K tokens/min sustained, with elastic scaling to 200K tokens/min within burst windows (subject to final capacity commit).
5) Fallback policy: when burst pool is exhausted, requests fall back to lower-capacity model with 2x latency degradation but preserved throughput.

Next steps I suggest:
- Confirm whether the 120s rolling window is acceptable or if you want a shorter window (60s) to reduce over-provisioning.
- Ben to send a short SRE checklist (network ports, keepalive, TLS termination) for your infra team.
- We can spin up a 2-week pilot with the proposed baseline and measure real-world session occupancy; Marissa can coordinate onboarding documentation.

I’ll wait for your confirmation on the burst window and whether we should proceed with the pilot config in the attached ratecard.

Thanks,

Laura Bennett
Account Executive | Redwood Inference
laura.bennett@redwood.com | +1 (415) 555-0189
Redwood Inference

From: Kyle Mercer <kyle.mercer@finledger.com>

Cc: Priya Shah <priya.shah@finledger.com>, Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.com>
Date: Wed, 12 Jun 2029 12:31:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Post-demo: parallel connection SLAs & adaptive burst window proposal

Thanks Laura — and thanks for the clear summary. A few clarifying items from our ops team: 

- The 2,500 parallel spike number is worst-case; more typical peaks are ~1,200 for ~45s. We modeled a 90s safety window to be conservative.
- For streaming sessions: the 300 concurrent streams is within reason, but we need to ensure our internal WebSocket proxy supports the keepalive strategy you mentioned (we'll share proxy config).

Two questions: 
1) What happens to in-flight streaming sessions if the burst pool steps down? Is there a graceful degradation path (e.g., reduce chunk frequency)?
2) Is the burst pool charged differently (overage) vs reserved capacity? We need to model cost in our internal forecast.

Also looping in Priya for data retention and audit concerns — she may have tweaks to concurrency if we need stricter audit logging on long-running streams.

On the ratecard PDF, we'll take a pass and get back with CFO for preliminary cost approval by next Tue.

—Kyle

Laura / Kyle —

A couple of compliance notes from my side that affect quota decisions: 
- Audit logs: for streaming sessions we need to capture creation and termination events and retain metadata for 90 days. If a streaming session is migrated or failed-over, we need a trace id surfaced in the log.
- Data residency: certain payment flows must not cross regions; ensure model routing keeps EU-bound datasets in eu region (not applicable today but planning ahead).

On concurrency: 300 streaming sessions is fine; however, if the burst pool is elastic and can shift capacity across customers, we need a guarantee that critical settlement windows have a minimum reserved floor (e.g., 1,000 slots reserved for our account during 01:00–03:00 UTC batch). If Redwood can't reserve capacity for a window, we need a documented SLA credit path.

Happy to sign off on pilot once we have: (a) written confirmation of reserved floor during our nightly batch, (b) logging hooks for session trace ids, and (c) a clear overage pricing table.

—Priya

Subject: Re: Post-demo: parallel connection SLAs & adaptive burst window proposal — next steps

Kyle / Priya —

Appreciate the quick feedback. Below are concrete answers and an updated pilot proposal.

Answers to your questions:
- In-flight streaming sessions: we do not forcibly terminate in-flight streams when burst capacity steps down. Instead we mark new session acceptance as "degraded" and, for active streams, we can reduce chunk frequency (server-side pacing) to preserve partial delivery while protecting overall SLOs. We'll provide a small SDK hook that lets your client toggle chunk frequency on signal.
- Billing: reserved baseline (500 sustained slots + 300 streaming slots) billed as committed capacity per month. Burst pool consumption during the pilot is billed as overage at the rate in the attached ratecard (line item: burst-slot-minute). We included an example cost calc in the PDF.
- Reserved floor during batch window: we can reserve a time-bound floor of 1,000 slots for your nightly 01:00–03:00 UTC if you commit to a 3-month pilot minimum. This will be a contractual setting in the Dedicated capacity agreement and enforced by routing priority. SLA credits apply if enforced routing fails (standard SLA table in the contract).

Updated pilot configuration (what we'll provision once you approve):
- Committed: 500 ephemeral parallel request slots; 300 streaming sessions reserved.
- Time-bound reserve: 1,000 slot floor between 01:00–03:00 UTC (nightly batch) for the pilot window.
- Burst pool: 2,000 slots with 120s rolling window; auto-fallback to lower-capacity model when exhausted.
- Observability: token-level tracing, session trace ids surfaced as header X-RD-Trace for your logs, and an endpoint to pull session lifecycle events (we'll provide a short webhook or S3 dump depending on your preference).

Next steps (action owners):
- Ben Carter (Redwood) to send SRE checklist + keeper config (eta: EOD Thu).
- Priya to confirm audit log retention format and preferred delivery (webhook vs S3).
- Kyle to review attached ratecard with finance; confirm cost approval by next Tue (18 Jun).
- Laura to open a pilot service request and draft the dedicated pilot commitment document.

If that all looks good, we'll schedule a quick (30 min) handshake with your infra team to set up credentials and network peering.

Thanks —

Laura Bennett
Account Executive | Redwood Inference
